title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Madison Heights files the first site plan while communities push back on power and water demands.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we start with the first formal site plan filing in Madison Heights, the latest sign that these projects are moving from talk to paper across the state.
That filing in Oakland County really puts a face on what residents 30 miles away might start feeling soon.
Exactly. Let's unpack what this means for power lines, water systems, and the bigger pattern of pushback we've seen all week.
Graham, walk me through the Madison Heights filing itself. What do we know happened today?
Officials received a formal site plan for a data center in that Oakland County suburb. It's the first concrete step toward construction there.
And the ripple effects? The summary mentioned strain on local power lines and water even for people farther out.
Right. If it advances, added demand could hit transmission and treatment capacity that serves a wider area, not just the immediate neighbors.
How does this fit into the history of these fights? It feels like every township is reacting differently now.
We've seen a wave of responses this past week alone. Wixom advanced new restrictions yesterday despite a lawsuit threat from developers.
And on Saturday Ellington Township approved a moratorium to give locals time to study power, water, and tax impacts.
Genesee County got its own impact study delivered the same day. Officials there now have specifics on strain to roads, utilities, and taxpayers.
So Madison Heights is sort of the flip side — a project stepping forward while others are hitting the brakes. Who are the main players here?
Developers pushing the plans, local planning commissions reviewing site plans, and residents organized around utility rates and land use. State regulators are in the mix too on the power side.
What about the electric bills angle? We keep hearing data centers as a driver for rate requests.
DTE asked for a big hike on Friday, and the attorney general wants it cut by 71 percent because it would hit households too hard. Data center demand is cited as one reason behind the ask.
That ties directly to the two new gas plants DTE is seeking to build, also from Thursday. Those would feed the growing load but could mean more fossil generation and higher costs.
Residents from Detroit out to Ann Arbor would feel that through rates. The plants come as older coal units retire, so the timing is tight.
Water use is another piece that keeps coming up. How big a deal is that for places like Madison Heights?

Cooling systems at scale pull serious volumes. Townships are already rewriting zoning to address it, like the two more Metro Detroit suburbs that changed codes on Thursday after noise and water concerns.
And farmland or open space? These projects often go on large parcels.

The Saline Township proposal is still advancing despite new rules and pushback. It could bring construction jobs but also heavy demands on power and water that affect property values and taxes nearby.
New state bills were introduced on Friday to regulate large builds with rules on power, noise, and tax deals. How might those change the game?
They respond to the growing local pushback and could add oversight that slows or shapes future campuses. Lawmakers are clearly watching the same trend we are.
What happens next in Madison Heights specifically? Is this filing the start of a long review process?
Yes. Site plan review usually means public hearings, traffic studies, utility capacity checks, and possible conditions before any shovels move. Residents will have chances to weigh in.
And if it clears locally, state utility regulators still have a say on interconnection and rates.
Exactly. The bigger pattern is communities buying time with moratoriums and studies while projects like this one test the current rules.
We also saw a recall effort fail on Friday against officials who approved a big rezoning. That keeps a 500-acre project on track in a divided community.
Right. Opponents now face a steeper climb to force another vote. It shows how these decisions can stick even when sentiment is split.
So for listeners 30 miles away, the takeaway is that one filing can influence regional infrastructure planning even if the site isn't in their backyard.
That's the thread running through all of this. Power and water systems don't stop at township lines.
Graham, any sense of how many places have paused or tightened rules so far this summer?
From what we've tracked, at least a handful in Oakland, Tuscola, and Genesee counties have acted in recent days, with more zoning changes in the works.
And the Genesee study gives leaders concrete numbers on potential taxpayer hits. Other counties might follow that model.
It does. The study details strain on power, water, and roads, giving residents elsewhere a template for what to ask.
What should people watch for in the coming weeks on the Madison Heights project?
Next steps would be any planning commission meetings or public comment periods once the filing is reviewed. Those are where details on size and utility needs usually surface.
And on the state level, how the new bills move could set the tone for all these local fights.
We'll keep tracking both. Now let's hit the other stories from the past few days in quick hits.
Yesterday in Wixom, officials moved new restrictions forward even with a lawsuit threat from developers. That could cap big power and water draws in Oakland County.
Residents there might see shifts in taxes, traffic, and utility rates depending on what gets built.
Saturday brought the Ellington Township moratorium in Tuscola County. Locals now have breathing room to examine demands before anything advances.
Nearby communities will watch how that plays out for their own planning.
Also Saturday, the Genesee panel handed over its impact study. Officials have the details on power, water, and road strain for taxpayers.
That gives residents in surrounding areas a model for scrutiny on similar proposals.
On Friday, Attorney General Nessel pushed for a big cut to DTE's rate hike request, citing household impacts and data center demand as a factor.
A smaller increase would still mean higher bills, but it shows the pushback at the regulatory level.
New bills targeting data center rules also dropped Friday, focusing on power use, noise, and tax deals.
That legislative response lines up with the local actions we've seen.
The recall effort against officials who approved a major rezoning failed on Friday, keeping that 500-acre project moving.
Opponents are now in a tougher spot to change course.
Saline Township's project is still pushing ahead despite tightened zoning and pushback. Jobs versus utility demands is the tension there.
Ripple effects on rates and taxes could reach well beyond the township.
Thursday DTE signaled plans for two new gas plants to meet data center demand, which could raise bills and shift generation.
From Detroit to Ann Arbor, that's the kind of infrastructure decision that lands on customer statements.
And two more Metro Detroit towns changed zoning on Thursday to curb projects over noise, water, and power concerns.
Those changes could slow or block what developers had eyed in the region.
Graham, anything on deck for meetings listeners can attend?
No specific public meetings listed for tonight on the tracker, but local planning commissions often post agendas weekly. Check your township site for upcoming reviews.
Always good to stay ahead of those comment periods.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Madison Heights Submits First Data Center Site Plan as Rules Tighten Statewide
